title: Being and Time
author: Martin Heidegger
edition_analyzed: Macquarrie & Robinson English translation (1962) — most widely referenced edition in scholarship
target_audience: Advanced students and scholars of philosophy
Readers interested in existentialism and continental philosophy
Those seeking to understand the foundations of modern existential thought
core_themes: Temporality and the structure of time
Care (Sorge) as a fundamental mode of being
The critique of metaphysics and traditional ontology
primary_purpose: To radically re-examine the question of what it means ‘to be’ by investigating human existence (Dasein), and to lay the groundwork for a new approach to ontology rooted in phenomenology and existential analysis.

structure_format.narrative_style: Rigorous, technical, and abstract philosophical prose
structure_format.organization: Divided into two main parts (only the first completed), with systematic sequential chapters (divisions and subsections) that build complex concepts step by step
features: Innovative terminology (e.g., Dasein, Being-in-the-world, thrownness, Being-toward-death)
Limited use of examples, focusing on conceptual clarity and critique of past philosophy

key_concepts_lessons: ‘Being’ is the most fundamental and yet most neglected question in philosophy.
Dasein (the human being as ‘being-there’) is unique in that it can question its own existence.
We are always already ‘being-in-the-world’, embedded in practical contexts and relationships.
Authenticity arises when individuals confront their own mortality and make choices true to themselves rather than to social convention (‘the they’).
Time (temporality) is central to the structure of existence: understanding ourselves as beings stretching toward possibilities and facing our finitude.
Traditional metaphysics has obscured the true nature of Being by treating it as a static, objective presence.
notable_features: Introduces many concepts foundational to existentialism and phenomenology
Profound influence on 20th-century philosophy, literature, theology, and psychology
Incomplete as originally intended (Heidegger never finished ‘Part Two’)
Features extensive neologisms and conceptual innovations
cultural_historical_context: Written in post-World War I Germany, 'Being and Time' marked a key turning point in 20th-century philosophy, challenging both the scientific rationalism of the age and the metaphysical traditions of Western thought. It responded to intellectual currents in phenomenology (especially Husserl), existential anxiety, and a perceived crisis in meaning.
reception_impact: Regarded as one of the most significant philosophical works of the 20th century
Foundational for existentialism, influencing Sartre, Merleau-Ponty, Beauvoir, and many others
Catalyst for later debates in hermeneutics (Gadamer), deconstruction (Derrida), and existential psychotherapy
Notoriously difficult reading; both revered for its depth and criticized for opacity and jargon
Subject of ongoing debate due to Heidegger’s later politics and relationship to Nazism
comparable_titles: Being and Nothingness by Jean-Paul Sartre
Phenomenology of Perception by Maurice Merleau-Ponty
Ideas: General Introduction to Pure Phenomenology by Edmund Husserl
The Courage to Be by Paul Tillich
Introduction to Metaphysics by Martin Heidegger
